📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success.

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here.

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

Recent findings suggest that we then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:.

Recent findings suggest that double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:.

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Industry observers note that not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a substantial catalyst for Jack,” Adam noted. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”.

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

In a recent development, the 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”.

Industry observers note that blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he states he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he remarked.

Sources indicate that the 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Car parking (one per four guests) is also included, adding convenience to this enhanced match experience.

In a recent development, manchester City's seven-match winning run to start the Premier League campaign feels like a very long time ago. Three successive defeats before the international break have left Enzo Maresca's side six points behind leaders Arsenal, while they also trail early-season surprise package Brighton & Hove Albion.

The good news for City is that Fulham appear to be the perfect opponent to end their losing streak. They have beaten the Cottagers in each of the last 20 meetings in all competitions, while their unbeaten run stretches back 26 games to a 3-1 home defeat in April 2009 — the first season under the Abu Dhabi United Group ownership.

A win would see City narrow the gap to Arsenal ahead of the Gunners' trip to Newcastle United later in the day, giving them a psychological boost for their clash with Mikel Arteta's side at the Emirates Stadium next weekend.

Winger Antoine Semenyo remains absent with a knee injury, while defenders Marc Guehi and Abdukodir Khusanov are doubtful after withdrawing from international duty due to fitness issues.

Fulham will feel like this is as good a time as any to change their appalling record against City, on account of their opponents' recent vulnerabilities and their own encouraging run of form.

The Cottagers followed up wins over Hull City and Coventry City with draws against Aston Villa and Newcastle United before the international break, easing the pressure on manager Alvaro Arbeloa.

Fulham's unbeaten run has lifted them to 15th in the Premier League and a rare win at the Etihad Stadium would propel them all the way up to 10th, for a few hours at least.

Sources indicate that midfielder Tom Cairney could return for the Cottagers, but goalkeeper Benjamin Lecomte is out for the season with an Achilles injury. Emile Smith Rowe also looks set to miss today's game with a hip matter.

The international break should have allowed City to reset so we are backing them to return to winning ways.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Luca Williams-Barnett lived up to the hype with a sparking display on his full debut for Tottenham to inspire a 2-0 win over Ipswich.

Roberto De Zerbi turned to the 18-year-old after two bright cameos and the highly-rated Spurs attacker delivered with aplomb, scoring on his first Premier League start after 15 minutes before a mazy run set up Dominic Solanke at the start of the second half.

After Williams-Barnett made his senior debut at the age of 16 last season, the clamour for the teenager to play has only increased during a difficult last 12 months and with injuries to Mathys Tel and Mykhailo Mudryk, the England Under-19 international grasped his chance to show why he has been hailed as a “special talent” by De Zerbi.

It was not a completely positive afternoon for De Zerbi with Savio forced off late on with a problem on his comeback after a seven-week lay-off.

However, this victory made it three home wins in a row for Tottenham in the Premier League for the first time in two years in further evidence a corner may have been turned in N17.

The excitement was palpable when it was confirmed Williams-Barnett would earn a first start for Tottenham with De Zerbi making six changes from the defeat at Leeds.

Gary O’Neil also shuffled his pack and went to a back five, but Ipswich started strongly and Antonin Kinsky was forced to deny Abdoul Ouattara and Zian Flemming in quick succession.

With De Zerbi in the stand due to a touchline ban, Spurs slowly started to get on top with Solanke curling wide before Williams-Barnett had the crowd on their feet with two dangerous crosses after lightning-quick step-overs.

Solanke went close again with a header across goal before Christian Walton denied the Tottenham forward from another set-piece, but the breakthrough arrived in 15th minute and via teenage sensation Williams-Barnett.

Pedro Porro was the architect with a wonderful cross from the right-hand side and Williams-Barnett showed excellent hunger to get ahead of Ouattara before he bundled in with his left knee.

It made Williams-Barnett the youngest Tottenham scorer in the Premier League since Gareth Bale in 2007.

Spurs almost made it 2-0 by the half hour mark but Mohammed Kudus curled a fine free-kick against a post.

Ipswich threatened again soon after; the busy Conor Gallagher blocking an effort by Exequiel Palacios before Kinsky claimed a corner and James Maddison received a booking for a pull back on Julio Enciso.

There was still time for Williams-Barnett to have a header saved and Walton thwarted a Maddison curler before the break.

With the game still in the balance, Spurs required a second goal and Williams-Barnett stepped up to make the difference again in the 52nd minute.

After Williams-Barnett picked up the ball inside his own half, the 18-year-old raced past Darnell Furlong and sent across an inch-perfect cross for Solanke to slide home his third goal this season.

Williams-Barnett accepted the acclaim before he left to a standing ovation with 26 minutes left.

After Walton prevented an own-goal by Ipswich captain Dara O’Shea, a minute’s applause in memory of Danny Kelly followed in the 69th minute and whilst Savio was forced off not long after his cross hit a post, Tottenham made it four wins in five.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement1, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g. oxidative addition and reductive elimination). The widespread exploitation of systems based on main-group elements therefore requires alternative elementary steps to effect turnover. Herein, we demonstrate a new catalytic platform for nucleophilic fluorination, which exploits a complex based on calcium (the fifth most Earth-abundant element) as the fluoride delivery vehicle. The key intermediate is a calcium-fluoride complex featuring a terminal Ca–F interaction, a unique structural geometry enabled by a highly sterically encumbered dianionic ligand-scaffold. This intermediate links reactants and products through F– capture and release steps, and thereby unlocks catalytic F– shuttling. Late Ca–F bond breaking in the rate-determining fluoride-delivery transition-state means that electronic and steric tuning of F– by calcium is chemically significant; proof-of-concept results show a hitherto unprecedented level of selectivity for substitution over elimination brought about by Ca-modulation. In a broader context, this work demonstrates how control over catalyst speciation and reagent binding affinity are key factors for the future development of sustainable non-transition metal paradigms in catalysis.

Kieran Gibbs recalls his infamous Chelsea red card

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversial refereeing decisions have been a part of football for a long as the game has been around, but one of the most bizarre incidents in recent memory occurred during Arsenal’s infamous 6-0 defeat to Chelsea in March 2014.

After spotting an Arsenal handball on the goal line, referee Andrer Marriner reached for his pocket and flashed a red card to Kieran Gibbs.

However, the matter here was that it was actually Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain who had handled the ball, and in this pre-VAR era, Gibbs was forced into an early bath, despite the protests of players from both sides.

As Gibbs looks back on the incident more than a decade on, he remembers the confusion, the frustration and the surreal nature of the incident which wouldn’t be allowed to happen these days.

“It feels like a blur now, and it did at the time too,” he reflects to FourFourTwo. “It’s heated in the moment and you’re trying to focus on the game.”.

The incident came during a calamitous first half for the Gunners, who found themselves 2-0 down after just seven minutes in what was Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game in charge of the club.

The handball incident came in the 17th minute, when Oxlade-Chamberlain threw his left hand at an Eden Hazard shot, tipping it around the post. Marriner pointed to the spot and the referee was not for turning, despite widespread protests from both sets of players.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Belgian would slot home the penalty to effectively end the game as a contest, with Gibbs still finding it remarkable that such an incident would occur, given the technology now used in the game.

“It feels crazy that there was no VAR, because you don’t have those kinds of issues anymore,” he continues.

“It was a surreal and very frustrating moment that was unique in the Premier League, so it brought a lot of attention.

“Both captains and the referee were telling me I was definitely going off.

“After a few minutes of protesting, I needed to listen to them.

“It was a big error from the referee, who apologised later and the red card was rescinded.”.

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

  • Bournemouth extended their winning run to nine in all competitions as Evanilson scored for the sixth Premier League game in a row in a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth extended their winning run to nine in all competitions as Evanilson scored for the sixth Premier League game in a row in a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.

Justin Kluivert was also on target to help Marco Rose’s Cherries climb up to the dizzying heights of fourth place in the table.

The defeat means Forest are only above the relegation places on goal difference having failed to build on the momentum of their 3-1 win over Manchester City before the international break.

In a recent development, both teams started the game on the front foot and Forest had the first sight of goal. Neco Williams nodded dangerously across the face of goal at the far post, but Liam Delap was beaten to the ball by home defender Antonio Silva.

Evanilson was denied by a brilliant last-ditch tackle from Forest centre-back Jair Cunha before Marcus Tavernier’s 20-yard curler was well saved by Matz Sels.

Bournemouth took the lead through Evanilson in the 19th minute. James Hill cushioned a header into the path of Evanilson, and the in-form Brazilian took one touch before blasting a left-footed shot into the roof of the net.

Kluivert almost doubled the home side’s lead with an effort from the edge of the penalty area which sailed narrowly over the crossbar.

Evanilson then failed to keep his shot down after a long throw from Hill caused chaos in the Forest penalty area.

Oliver Glasner’s side had a penalty appeal waved away when Adam Smith blocked Williams’s effort into the arm of team-mate Tyler Adams.

Kluivert did make it 2-0 on the stroke of half-time with a simple far-post finish after a superb run and cross from Tavernier.

Forest were much improved in the second half, adopting a more direct approach in a bid to forage a way back into the game.

Delap turned provider by whipping in a cross for captain Morgan Gibbs-White but the England international could not properly connect with his header.

James McAtee ballooned an effort over the crossbar as the visitors continued to misfire in front of goal.

Substitute Chris Wood also miscued a header from a corner when he should have at least tested underworked Bournemouth goalkeeper Dorde Petrovic.

Bournemouth always looked a threat on the counter and Kluivert came close to his second and the Cherries’ third when he stung the gloves of Selz from 18 yards out.

Kluivert should also have been more clinical when he found himself within finishing range but unselfishly laid the ball off to Rayan and the chance went begging.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

In a recent development, an anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling fresh heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

Industry observers note that "But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it.".

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," states Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible.".

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Sources indicate that wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

It has been revealed that "That was our best performance," indicates Coleman. "We were awesome.".

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on.".

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

Recent findings suggest that "I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it.".

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," indicates James.

It has been revealed that "We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations.".

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space.".

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

It has been revealed that then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu states. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition.".

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour.".

Recent findings suggest that belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere.".

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'.".

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really key moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

Sources indicate that "That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game.".

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

Recent findings suggest that "I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and remarked things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football.".

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

Industry observers note that "Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed.".

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," claims Ledley.

Industry observers note that "Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone states, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'.".

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening.".

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

It has been revealed that this is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Recent findings suggest that asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.

The Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure. Tuesday’s final Nations League group match, at home to Kosovo, presents a chance for progress or yet another opportunity to showcase a frustrating habit of messing things up.

According to recent reports, for 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years. Set up in a compact, attack-minded formation they carried credible threat against hosts managed by Ralf Rangnick, but to nobody’s great surprise Sasa Kalajdzic broke the deadlock, scrambling home the winner from a needlessly conceded and poorly defended corner.

This late lapse neatly captures the contradiction bedevilling this Ireland team under Hallgrímsson. Over the past 12 months, Ireland have been unmistakably better than they were during the dark days of the post-pandemic slump under Stephen Kenny. They have established a clear identity and pulled off a couple of phenomenal wins with a spine of players performing at an elite level, supplemented by emerging talent from the leagues below and beyond. Yet for all that, an acceptable level of success remains elusive for a team who have not managed to shake a maddening habit of self-sabotage.

It has been revealed that they have a high ceiling, as they demonstrated a year ago. Last November they dismantled Portugal at the Aviva Stadium in a World Cup qualifier before booking their place in the playoffs with an unforgettable come-from-behind win against Hungary at the Puskas Arena.

According to recent reports, in Budapest, the celebrations of a dramatic Troy Parrott hat-trick completed in the sixth minute of added time went viral and elevated the then AZ striker from being surplus to the requirements of a dreadful Tottenham to sought-after European household name. For the first time in almost a decade, Ireland were playing with something resembling swagger, spearheaded by a poster-boy striker apparently entering his prime.

Industry observers note that riding that wave, Ireland travelled to Prague last March for the playoff semi-final against Czechia, with Parrott striking again, from the penalty spot, as they set about taking an early 2-0 lead. What followed would become the lowest point of Hallgrímsson’s reign as Ireland sat back and invited pressure before conceding a needless penalty and subsequent late equaliser that preceded a crushing shootout defeat. Despite last summer’s expanded 48-team format in North America, poor game management had stymied Ireland’s chances of making the cut.

In a recent development, an uninspiring, but unbeaten, summer friendly window featured fairly routine low-profile wins over Grenada and Qatar and a 1-1 draw against the World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal. Having steadied the ship before this Nations League campaign, Ireland produced a performance in their opener against Kosovo little short of diabolical and went down to another late goal.

In the subsequent four fixtures, two overshadowed by loud protests over Ireland’s decision to honour matches against Israel, that same cycle of promise and frustration has played out on a loop.

The disappointment of defeat in Pristina was immediately cancelled out by a clinical dispatch of Israel in Debrecen. In Dublin, against Austria, Parrott struck twice to give Ireland a commanding first-half lead, but in a collapse that rather mirrored their nightmarish Prague experience, Ireland went on to relinquish control and were forced to settle for a disappointing draw.

Three days later they coughed up another lead in a bad-tempered 1-1 draw with Israel, their compulsion for throwing away cheap points from winning positions coming back to bite them. Although they never led against Austria on Saturday, when Caoimhín Kelleher made a series of excellent saves, the winner they conceded was ridiculously soft.

Industry observers note that hallgrímsson’s appointment in July 2024 after a drawn-out process lasting eight months came as a surprise. He has built a side with a strong, if occasionally gaffe-prone, backbone including Kelleher, the goalkeeper’s Brentford teammate Nathan Collins and the Ipswich defender Dara O’Shea. Jack Moylan, having the season of his life at Cardiff, has impressed in midfield, and Southampton’s Finn Azaz is an occasional, but unreliable, source of creative guile. Parrott, enjoying life in La Liga with Real Betis, has evolved from promising talent to undisputed focal point of the attack.

Sources indicate that to his credit, Hallgrímsson has forged a clear, pragmatic identity that maximises his team’s strengths without any delusions of fancy-dan footballing grandeur against elite opposition. Under his watch, Ireland are rarely outclassed and carry a cutting edge sorely absent in the dying days of his predecessor’s tenure.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, an inability to concentrate for 90 minutes continues to be their undoing and the must-win Nations League group finale at the Aviva Stadium will provide the ultimate judgment on the past 12 months. With Austria guaranteed promotion to League A, Ireland still have second place and its promotion playoff spot within reach.

Industry observers note that victory over Kosovo would also secure a place in pot two for next month’s Euro qualifying draw in Belfast, whereas defeat could leave them flirting with a relegation playoff to the tournament’s third tier. As the only ever-present residents of the Nations League’s second tier, now may be the time for something finally to give.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa and Sunderland drew a blank in their Premier League match at Villa Park.

Unai Emery’s team had the better of a game of few chances but failed to make the breakthrough and are now without a win in five games in all competitions.

Sunderland, bidding to move away from the relegation zone, ended a run of three successive away defeats with the 0-0 draw.

Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Emiliano Buendia returned for Villa at the expense of Victor Lindelof and John McGinn, who was on the bench.

Sunderland also made two changes, with Jules Ahoka and Wilson Isidor replacing the injured Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey.

The home side were on the front foot from the off and forced a couple of early corners, which came to nothing.

They had to wait until the 19th minute for their first chance, with Johan Manzambi’s low effort saved by Robin Roefs.

The Sunderland goalkeeper had a let-off in the 40th minute when he gifted possession to Buendia but recovered to claim the Villa midfielder’s weak shot.

Ian Maatsen threatened to break the deadlock in the early stages of the second half, but he could only follow an impressive run with a shot straight at Roefs.

Soon after the Black Cats, who created little of note before half-time, forced their first corner but failed to produce anything worthwhile from it.

Villa’s Leon Goretzka was then booked for pulling back Chemsdine Talbi, but Enzo Le Fee’s free-kick evaded Nordi Mukiele and was collected by goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

As Villa fans chanted for the introduction of McGinn, Le Fee fired narrowly wide.

The home faithful got what they wanted just before the hour mark when McGinn was introduced, alongside Ibrahim Mbaye.

The Scotland international had a chance to open the scoring midway through the second half but fired over.

Sunderland won a free-kick 25 yards out when Goretzka fouled Le Fee, but the midfielder’s effort was straight at Suzuki.

Villa boss Emery made another double substitution in the 73rd minute, with Brian Madjo and Ross Barkley replacing Nicolas Jackson and Goretzka.

The home side pressed for a winner and, after McGinn failed to find the target three minutes later, Barkley forced Roefs to tip over a powerful effort from distance.

Roefs reacted sharply to prevent Mukiele heading into his own goal, then Alysson fired over.

The visitors almost stole a win in the first of three added minutes, but Talbi’s curling right-foot effort went narrowly wide of Suzuki’s far post.

Life as a Wag in the transfer window

📅 08 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour.
  • In a recent development, owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away.
  • Industry observers note that and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital.".

In a recent development, owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

Industry observers note that and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," notes Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age.".

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

In a recent development, "I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she claims. "We just met and we clicked.".

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to swiftly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," states Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she claims.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" claims Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she indicates.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

Recent findings suggest that "I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control.".

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it.".

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season.

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Industry observers note that last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is at the moment a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he claims he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

Recent findings suggest that "There's always the risk that a move might not work," he states. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere.".

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier.

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines.

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship.

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham.

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle.

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved.".

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us.".

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica states.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she notes.

In a recent development, "But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved.".

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football.".

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

Sources indicate that "You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

According to recent reports, "Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative.".

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," indicates Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she states.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place.".

She states they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," notes Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

It has been revealed that "The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the newly introduced strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing.".

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his upcoming clubs.

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you.".

Being sensible financially is also key.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she indicates. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control.".

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"In football, you don't get bored!".

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

📅 04 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
  • Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Industry observers note that watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

Industry observers note that the season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

Sources indicate that as demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology organization Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

It has been revealed that kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Sources indicate that through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

Recent findings suggest that "I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he indicates. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

Industry observers note that "When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he states. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

Sources indicate that distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a massive strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

It has been revealed that the Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

According to recent reports, karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

Sources indicate that with the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Chelsea missed the chance to open up a four-point gap at the top of the Women’s Super League having been held to a goalless draw by Liverpool.

Sonia Bompastor’s side remain unbeaten this season but their advantage over Manchester City, who play Sunday, is only two points after failing to find a way past Khiara Keating in St Helens.

The Liverpool goalkeeper tipped over Alyssa Thompson’s shot and also denied Sandy Baltimore at full stretch in the first half, before keeping out Wieke Kaptein, Keira Walsh and Sjoeke Nusken in the second.

Liverpool had ended a five-match run without a win with victory at Brighton last weekend and they carried that confidence into the game against the league leaders to move up to eighth.

"I am really pleased,” Liverpool manager Gareth Taylor remarked. “The girls stuck to the game proposal phenomenally well against a tough opponent and I cannot give them enough credit for what they did today. A lot of top individual performances and as a collective we really stuck to the task.

According to recent reports, "They had some chances, we had some chances - ours were probably better. And then in the second half, we didn't have the same amount because it's fatiguing to replicate that pressure and at times we didn't keep the ball well enough.

“But credit to the players. I am so pleased they held on as sometimes you need that just for all your work.”.

Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ claims Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.
  • Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead.
  • The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ claims Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he stated, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

It has been revealed that against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

Industry observers note that as in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he noted, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”.

According to recent reports, the parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

According to recent reports, the score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a significant game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

Recent findings suggest that “We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel noted. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”.

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, stated England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”.

Sources indicate that tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

According to recent reports, “It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

It has been revealed that “The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were newly introduced in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was vital to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

Sources indicate that “We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”.

#105387. Tech Report: Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win
